found-terminology-l01.q: You are handed the parts my/o, cardi/o and -itis and told to build the word for inflammation of the heart muscle. Which spelling follows the combining vowel rule?
found-terminology-l01.why: Between two roots the combining vowel stays, so my/o keeps its o before cardi. The next part, -itis, begins with a vowel, so cardi drops its o. Myocardioitis keeps a vowel before a vowel, mycarditis drops a vowel that belongs between two roots, and myoocarditis doubles it.

found-terminology-l01.q: A note reads myelopathy. A student reads it as muscle disease. What is the error?
choices: Nothing, my/o and myel/o are the same root
Myel/o means spinal cord or bone marrow, not muscle
Myel/o means nerve, so it should read neuropathy
found-terminology-l01.why: My/o is muscle and myel/o is spinal cord or bone marrow; the extra letters change the organ entirely. -pathy does mean disease, and nerve is neur/o, so the only mistake is the root.

found-terminology-l02.q: A chart says the patient is followed by nephrology for chronic kidney disease and has a stent in the renal artery. Why are two different kidney words used in one sentence?
choices: Nephrology is the specialty and renal is the artery's own name, unrelated to kidney
Greek nephr/o builds disease and specialty names while Latin ren/o builds adjectives
Renal refers only to the left kidney
found-terminology-l02.why: Medicine kept both the Greek and the Latin root for kidney. Greek nephr/o shows up in nephrology, nephritis and nephrectomy; Latin ren/o shows up as the adjective renal. Same organ, two vocabularies, and renal is not side specific.

found-terminology-l02.q: A handwritten note could read hepatoma or hematoma. Why does the difference matter?
choices: One is a liver tumor and the other is a collected pocket of blood
They mean the same thing spelled two ways
One is a blood tumor and the other is a liver infection
Both mean bleeding into the liver
found-terminology-l02.why: Hepat/o is liver and hemat/o is blood, and -oma is a mass. A hepatoma is a liver tumor; a hematoma is a pocket of blood in tissue. They are neither synonyms nor two versions of one problem, and neither word contains an inflammation suffix.

found-terminology-l03.q: A patient with a gallbladder problem has cholecystitis, and a patient with a bladder infection has cystitis. What does this tell you about cyst/o?
choices: Cyst/o always means bladder and cholecystitis is an exception in name only
Cyst/o means any fluid-filled sac, and the neighboring root decides which sac
Cyst/o means stone in one word and bladder in the other
Cyst/o means inflammation in both words
found-terminology-l03.why: Cyst/o means bladder or any fluid-filled sac. In cholecystitis the neighbor chol/e (bile) makes it the gallbladder; alone in cystitis it is the urinary bladder. Lith/o is stone and -itis is inflammation, so neither meaning belongs to cyst/o.

found-terminology-l03.q: Which term describes vomiting blood rather than coughing it up?
found-terminology-l03.why: -emesis is vomiting, so hematemesis is vomiting blood. Hemoptysis is coughing up blood from the airway, hemothorax is blood in the chest cavity, and hematuria is blood in the urine.

found-terminology-l04.q: An adult patient has a heart rate of 112 and a respiratory rate of 8. Which pair of terms belongs in the chart?
found-terminology-l04.why: Adult tachycardia is over 100, so 112 qualifies. Adult bradypnea is under 12, so 8 qualifies. Nothing here is slow in the heart or fast in the breathing, which rules out the other three combinations.

found-terminology-l04.q: A medication is ordered to be given between the ribs, and another is ordered into the muscle. Which prefixes name those two routes?
choices: Inter- for between the ribs and intra- for into the muscle
Intra- for between the ribs and inter- for into the muscle
Infra- for between the ribs and intro- for into the muscle
Both are intra-, since they differ only by target
found-terminology-l04.why: Inter- means between, as in intercostal, and intra- means within, as in intramuscular. The two prefixes differ by one letter and are commonly swapped; infra- and intro- are not the prefixes in either word.

found-terminology-l05.q: A report describes rhinorrhea in one patient and hemorrhage in another. What is the difference the suffix is carrying?
choices: Both mean bleeding, from different sites
-rrhea is a flow or discharge while -rrhage is a bursting forth of blood
-rrhea is a burst and -rrhage is a slow drip
-rrhea means surgical repair and -rrhage means rupture
found-terminology-l05.why: -rrhea is a flow, as in a runny nose or diarrhea; -rrhage or -rrhagia is a bursting forth, meaning heavy bleeding. Rhinorrhea is not bleeding at all, and neither suffix has anything to do with surgical repair, which is -plasty.

found-terminology-l05.q: A patient is scheduled for a procedure whose name ends in -graphy. What is being produced?
choices: The process of recording an image
found-terminology-l05.why: -graphy is the process of recording, as in angiography, and -gram is the record itself. -plasty is repair, -ostomy is a permanent opening, and -tome is a cutting instrument.

found-terminology-l06.q: A patient with severe difficulty breathing is placed with the head of the stretcher raised to 75 degrees. Which position is that?
found-terminology-l06.why: Fowler's is sitting upright at about 60 to 90 degrees, which is what a patient in respiratory distress usually chooses. Semi-Fowler's is 30 to 45 degrees, Trendelenburg is head-down, and left lateral recumbent is on the side.

found-terminology-l06.q: After splinting a forearm fracture you document distal pulses, motor and sensation intact. Why is the word distal doing the work in that sentence?
choices: It means the side away from midline
It means the deepest layer of tissue
It means the front surface of the limb
It means past the injury, farther from the trunk, which is where circulation would fail first
found-terminology-l06.why: Distal means farther from the point of attachment to the trunk, so checking distal to the splint proves the splint did not cut off circulation. Away from midline is lateral, deeper is deep, and the front surface is anterior.

found-terminology-l07.q: A 47-year-old has severe pain in the right upper quadrant an hour after a fried meal. Which organ is the first suspect?
found-terminology-l07.why: The gallbladder sits in the right upper quadrant and contracts after fatty food, which is the classic trigger. The appendix is right lower, the spleen is left upper, and the sigmoid colon is left lower.

found-terminology-l07.q: Which region name is used for the area just above the stomach in the upper middle abdomen, and why does pain there get an ECG?
choices: Hypogastric, because bladder pain can be cardiac
Umbilical, because the aorta lies behind it
Epigastric, because heart attacks commonly present as burning pain there
Right hypochondriac, because the liver refers pain to the chest
found-terminology-l07.why: Epigastric is the upper middle region, and myocardial infarction often presents as epigastric burning mistaken for indigestion, so an ECG is obtained early. Hypogastric is suprapubic, umbilical is central, and right hypochondriac is the liver and gallbladder area.

found-terminology-l08.q: A chart entry reads AMS, onset unclear. What single test should accompany that finding automatically?
found-terminology-l08.why: Altered mental status is always paired with a glucose check because hypoglycemia is common, fast to find, and immediately reversible. The other three tests may follow, but none is the automatic first pairing with AMS.

found-terminology-l08.q: A note reads s/p MVC, BIBA, GSW ruled out. Decode the three abbreviations in order.
choices: Status post, brought in by ambulance, gunshot wound
Seen post, by intake before admission, general surgical wound
Since presentation, brought in by air, great saphenous wound
Systolic pressure, bedside intake before assessment, gastric surgical wound
found-terminology-l08.why: s/p is status post, meaning after; BIBA is brought in by ambulance; GSW is gunshot wound. The other expansions are invented and none of them are in routine use.

found-terminology-l09.q: Which of these four written orders is safe as written?
choices: Morphine sulfate 2 mg IV q4h PRN pain
found-terminology-l09.why: The morphine order spells the drug name in full, has no trailing zero, and uses a written frequency. U for unit, a missing leading zero before .075, QD for daily, and a trailing zero after 5 are each on the do-not-use list.

found-terminology-l09.q: A pharmacy technician asks why cc is discouraged when everyone knows it means milliliter. What is the actual reason?
choices: It is a metric unit that is no longer defined
Handwritten cc can be read as u, meaning unit
It is only valid for solids, not liquids
It is a thousandfold larger than a milliliter
found-terminology-l09.why: The problem is visual, not mathematical: sloppy cc looks like u, which is the abbreviation for unit. A cubic centimeter equals a milliliter exactly, so the units are identical in size and still perfectly well defined.

found-terminology-l10.q: A chart lists leukocytosis in one patient and leukopenia in another. Which patient has too many white cells?
choices: The one with leukocytosis, because -osis is an abnormal condition, usually an excess
The one with leukopenia, because -penia means abundance
Both, since the two suffixes are synonyms
Neither, since leuk/o refers to platelets
found-terminology-l10.why: -osis is an abnormal condition, generally an excess, and -penia is a deficiency, so the two words are opposites. Leuk/o is white, meaning white blood cells, not platelets, which are thromb/o or the word platelet itself.

found-terminology-l10.q: A surgical schedule lists an ileostomy and an iliac crest bone graft on two different patients. What is the difference between ileum and ilium?
choices: They are two spellings of the same hip bone
Ileum is a hip bone and ilium is the last part of the small intestine
Ileum is the last part of the small intestine and ilium is the wide upper hip bone
Both refer to the pelvis, one anterior and one posterior
found-terminology-l10.why: The ileum is the final segment of the small intestine, so an ileostomy opens bowel onto the abdominal wall. The ilium is the broad flaring hip bone whose crest is a graft site. They sound identical and are not related.

found-terminology-l11.q: A blood gas reports pH 7.21, PaCO2 62, HCO3 24. Which number is the lung's contribution?
found-terminology-l11.why: PaCO2 is set by ventilation, so it is the lung's number, and here it is high, meaning carbon dioxide is being retained. HCO3 is the kidney's number and is normal, and pH is the overall result, not the source.

found-terminology-l11.q: A radiology impression ends with clinical correlation recommended. What is the radiologist saying?
choices: The study was technically inadequate and must be repeated
The image alone cannot settle the question, so the answer depends on the patient
An incidental finding was deliberately omitted
found-terminology-l11.why: Clinical correlation recommended means the picture is compatible with more than one story and the patient in front of you decides which. It is not a statement about image quality, it does not declare a finding benign, and nothing is being hidden.

found-terminology-l12.q: An order reads: Prednisone 20 mg PO BID x 5 days. How many tablets are dispensed?
found-terminology-l12.why: BID is twice daily, so two tablets a day for five days is ten. Five would be once daily, fifteen would be three times daily, and twenty would be four times daily.

found-terminology-l12.q: A sig line reads: Ondansetron 4 mg SL q8h. What is missing that must be queried rather than assumed?
found-terminology-l12.why: The order gives drug, strength, route and frequency but no indication and no duration or quantity. A missing element on an order is a question for the prescriber, never a blank you fill from memory.

found-terminology-l13.q: A patient has a needle placed to drain fluid from the abdominal cavity. Which procedure name fits?
found-terminology-l13.why: -centesis is a puncture to withdraw fluid, so draining the abdomen is paracentesis. A laparotomy opens the abdomen surgically, a colostomy creates a lasting opening of the colon, and a herniorrhaphy sews a hernia closed.

found-terminology-l13.q: A handoff says the patient is ORIF right femur, POD 2. What happened and when?
choices: The femur was amputated two days ago
The femur was imaged with contrast two days ago
The femur fracture was realigned and fixed with hardware, and this is the second day after surgery
The femur was fused to the pelvis two days ago
found-terminology-l13.why: ORIF is open reduction internal fixation: the bone is realigned through an incision and held with hardware. POD 2 is postoperative day two. Amputation is AKA or BKA, fusion is -desis, and imaging with contrast is not a surgical term.

found-terminology-l14.q: A head-injured patient's blood pressure is climbing, the heart rate is falling, and breathing has become irregular. What is this pattern called?
found-terminology-l14.why: Rising pressure, falling heart rate and irregular breathing is Cushing's triad, a sign of rising intracranial pressure. Beck's triad is tamponade, Kussmaul's sign is neck veins rising on inspiration, and Cheyne-Stokes names one breathing pattern rather than the whole triad.

found-terminology-l14.q: Two findings on the list are named after Kussmaul. What are they, and how are they related?
choices: A breathing pattern and a neck vein finding, which are unrelated to each other
Two names for the same acidotic breathing pattern
A breathing pattern and a skin bruising sign, both from pancreatitis
A neck vein finding and an ECG wave, both from hypothermia
found-terminology-l14.why: Kussmaul respirations are deep, fast, sighing breaths in metabolic acidosis; Kussmaul's sign is neck veins that rise on inspiration in tamponade or constrictive pericarditis. They share only a name. The hypothermia ECG wave is the Osborn or J wave.

found-terminology-l15.q: A handoff line reads: CP w/o radiation. A listener hears it as CP w/ radiation. Why does that single character matter?
choices: It changes the location of the pain from chest to arm
It changes whether the pain spreads, which changes how concerning the chest pain is
It changes the time of onset
It changes the route of the medication given
found-terminology-l15.why: w/ means with and w/o means without. Radiating chest pain raises concern for a cardiac cause, so dropping the o inverts the description. Location, timing and route are all carried by other parts of the line.

found-terminology-l15.q: Which run sheet format explicitly separates what the patient told you from what you measured?
found-terminology-l15.why: SOAP splits Subjective (what the patient says) from Objective (what you measured). CHART uses chief complaint, history, assessment, Rx and transport; SBAR is a handoff structure; MDM is a section of a physician note, not a narrative format.

found-terminology-l16.q: An emergency department patient has been admitted but is still in a department bed waiting for a floor bed. What is the standard operational term?
found-terminology-l16.why: A boarder is an admitted patient still occupying an emergency department bed. A bounce back returns soon after discharge, LWBS left without being seen, and AMA left against medical advice.

found-terminology-l16.q: Why does calling a patient a frequent flyer in a chart cause harm beyond being unprofessional?
choices: It biases the next assessment, and the next visit may be the one with a real emergency
It is a billing code that triggers an audit
It is protected by the record and never read by anyone else
It is medically accurate but poorly worded
found-terminology-l16.why: The label substitutes a judgment for a finding and lowers the care given at the next visit, which is exactly when the complaint may be real. Charts are also discoverable and read by patients, lawyers and boards, so the opposite of being private.

found-terminology-l17.q: A vignette describes a clot forming in a deep leg vein. Which system's root set should you pull first?
found-terminology-l17.why: A vein and a clot both belong to the cardiovascular file: thromb/o clot, phleb/o and ven/o vein. The respiratory, musculoskeletal and genitourinary sets name lungs, bones and the urinary tract, none of which the stem describes.

found-terminology-l17.q: Build the word for low sodium in the blood using the system file for endocrine and metabolic terms.
found-terminology-l17.why: Natr/o is sodium, so hypo- plus natr plus -emia is hyponatremia. Kal/i is potassium, calc/i is calcium, and glyc/o is sugar, so the other three name different substances entirely.

quiz.q: Which word is spelled correctly under the combining vowel rule?
quiz.why: Between the two roots oste/o and arthr/o the combining vowel stays, and before the vowel-initial suffix -itis the second root drops its vowel. Ostearthritis wrongly drops the vowel between roots, and the other two keep a vowel before a vowel.

quiz.q: A student sees the unfamiliar word splenorrhaphy on an operative note. Using the backwards method, what does it mean?
quiz.why: Decode suffix first: -rrhaphy is surgical suturing, and splen/o is spleen. Removal would be splenectomy, enlargement would be splenomegaly, and imaging would end in -graphy.

quiz.q: A handwritten note could be read as either hyperkalemia or hypokalemia. Why is this the most dangerous class of near-twin in medical language?
choices: The two words describe different electrolytes
The two words describe the same finding with different severity
The two words are opposites that call for opposite treatments
The two words differ only in which organ is involved
quiz.why: Hyper- is above normal and hypo- is below normal, so the same root yields opposite states and opposite management. Both words concern potassium in the blood, so the electrolyte and the organ are identical and severity is not the issue.

quiz.q: Which of these plurals is formed correctly?
quiz.why: Latin and Greek plurals are irregular: apex becomes apices, diagnosis becomes diagnoses, vertebra becomes vertebrae, and bronchus becomes bronchi. The three wrong options all apply an English -es ending to a non-English word.

quiz.q: A note reads: patient with cardiomyopathy admitted for evaluation. Which three parts is that word built from?
quiz.why: Cardiomyopathy is disease of the heart muscle: cardi/o plus my/o plus -pathy. Myel/o is cord or marrow and myc/o is fungus, neither of which appears here, and -pathy is disease, not inflammation or weakness.

quiz.q: A chart describes a patient with a colostomy and a second patient with colitis. Which structure do both terms involve?
quiz.why: Col/o and colon/o mean large intestine, so both words point there. Gastr/o is the stomach, enter/o is the small intestine, and cholecyst/o is the gallbladder.

quiz.q: A 58-year-old has a diagnosis of arteriosclerosis while a 58-year-old in the next bed has arthrosclerosis documented in error. What did the second word accidentally say?
choices: Hardening of a joint rather than of an artery
Hardening of an artery rather than of a joint
Inflammation of a joint rather than of an artery
Narrowing of a vein rather than of an artery
quiz.why: Arteri/o is artery and arthr/o is joint, and -sclerosis is hardening in both. The error swaps the target organ, not the process; inflammation would be -itis and narrowing would be -stenosis.

quiz.q: Encephal/o is a long root. What is it actually built from, and why does that help?
choices: En- meaning without plus cephal/o meaning brain
En- meaning inside plus cephal/o meaning head, so it names the thing inside the head
Encephal is a single unsplittable Greek word for nerve
Ence- meaning central plus phal/o meaning cord
quiz.why: En- is inside and cephal/o is head, so encephal/o literally names the organ inside the head, the brain. En- does not mean without, that is a- or an-, and there is no phal/o root for cord.

quiz.q: A patient with a kidney stone lodged in the ureter is described in the chart. Which term names the underlying condition?
quiz.why: Nephr/o kidney plus lith stone plus -iasis condition gives nephrolithiasis. Cholelithiasis is gallstones, nephrosclerosis is hardening of the kidney, and pyelonephritis is infection reaching the kidney.

quiz.q: A note documents purulent drainage and the term pyuria in the urinalysis comment. What does py/o mean?
quiz.why: Py/o is pus, so pyuria is pus in the urine. Fever is pyr/o as in antipyretic, renal pelvis is pyel/o, and there is no common root py/o for pressure.

quiz.q: A patient produces only 15 mL of urine over four hours. Which term belongs in the chart?
quiz.why: Olig- means few or scanty, so oliguria is scanty urine output. Poly- means many, so polyuria is the opposite; dysuria is painful urination, and hematuria is blood in the urine, neither of which is about volume.

quiz.q: A stroke patient can speak clearly but chokes on sips of water. Which term is correct?
quiz.why: Phag/o is swallowing, so dysphagia is difficulty swallowing. Phas/o is speech, so dysphasia and aphasia describe the speech problem this patient does not have, and dyspnea is difficult breathing.

quiz.q: A patient is described as having paraplegia after a spinal injury. Which pattern does that name?
choices: Weakness of one side of the body
quiz.why: Para- here means two like parts and -plegia is paralysis, giving paralysis of both legs. One-sided weakness is hemiparesis, all four limbs is quadriplegia, and a single limb would be monoplegia.

quiz.q: An ondansetron order is written to prevent vomiting. Which prefix explains why the drug class is called antiemetic?
quiz.why: Anti- means against, so an antiemetic opposes vomiting, just as an antipyretic opposes fever. Ante- means before as in antecubital timing terms, endo- is within, and auto- is self.

quiz.q: A note records that a patient has hepatomegaly. What was found?
quiz.why: -megaly is enlargement, so hepatomegaly is an enlarged liver. Inflammation would be hepatitis, a tumor would be hepatoma, and hardening would be a -sclerosis ending.

quiz.q: A patient describes constant pins and needles in both feet. Which term names that sensation?
quiz.why: -esthesia is sensation and para- marks it as abnormal, giving paresthesia. Paresis is weakness, paralysis is absent movement, and analgesia is absence of pain, which is a different finding entirely.

quiz.q: A surgical consent form lists an angioplasty. What will be done?
choices: A vessel will be repaired or reshaped
A vessel will be punctured to withdraw fluid
quiz.why: -plasty is surgical repair or reshaping, so angioplasty reshapes a narrowed vessel. Imaging is angiography, removal would be an -ectomy, and puncture to withdraw fluid is -centesis.

quiz.q: A resident says the patient has bacteremia, and a student charts active bleeding. What is the error?
choices: Bacteremia means a bacterial infection of a wound, not bleeding
-emia means a blood condition, so bacteremia is bacteria in the blood, not hemorrhage
Bacteremia means bacteria in the urine, not the blood
Bacteremia and hemorrhage are both correct descriptions
quiz.why: -emia names a condition of the blood, never an act of bleeding, so bacteremia is bacteria circulating in blood. Bleeding suffixes are -rrhage and -rrhagia. Bacteria in the urine would be bacteriuria, and wound infection has no -emia ending.

quiz.q: You are facing a patient who points to a wound on the side of the body nearest your right hand. How is it documented?
choices: Right side, because documentation uses the examiner's orientation
Left side, because left and right always belong to the patient
Lateral side, because sides are not named right or left
It depends on whether the patient is supine or prone
quiz.why: Left and right are always the patient's, so the side nearest your right hand when facing them is their left. The examiner's orientation is never used, sides are named, and position does not change whose left it is.

quiz.q: A patient in shock is about to be placed head-down in Trendelenburg by a new provider. What is the best response?
choices: Encourage it, since Trendelenburg is the standard shock position
Encourage it, since head-down positioning improves breathing
Point out that current evidence does not support it and follow local protocol instead
Substitute the prone position for all shock patients
quiz.why: Trendelenburg was taught for decades but is not supported by current evidence and can worsen breathing by pushing abdominal contents against the diaphragm; protocol governs. Prone is not a shock position and would compromise assessment and the airway.

quiz.q: A dorsalis pedis pulse is checked. Where is it found and what does dorsal mean here?
choices: Top of the foot, since dorsal means the back or upper surface, equivalent to posterior in the trunk
Sole of the foot, since dorsal means underneath
Behind the knee, since dorsal means proximal
Inner ankle, since dorsal means medial
quiz.why: Dorsal equals posterior in the trunk and names the upper surface of the foot, the dorsum, where the dorsalis pedis is palpated. The sole is plantar, behind the knee is the popliteal pulse, and the inner ankle carries the posterior tibial pulse.

quiz.q: An MRI is described as showing midsagittal images of the brain. What does that tell you about the slices?
choices: They divide the body into anterior and posterior parts
They divide the body into superior and inferior parts
They divide the body into equal left and right halves
They are taken at an oblique angle across the skull
quiz.why: A midsagittal or median cut runs vertically down the exact middle, creating equal left and right halves. Anterior and posterior division is frontal or coronal, superior and inferior is transverse, and oblique is not one of the three standard planes.

quiz.q: Which cavity holds the heart, lungs, great vessels and esophagus?
quiz.why: The thoracic cavity contains the heart, lungs, great vessels and esophagus, with the mediastinum as its central compartment. The abdominal cavity holds digestive organs, the cranial cavity holds the brain, and the pelvic cavity holds bladder and rectum.

quiz.q: A patient has left upper quadrant tenderness after being struck in the left lower ribs. Which organ is most likely injured?
quiz.why: The spleen sits in the left upper quadrant under the lower left ribs and is the classic organ injured by blunt force there. The liver and gallbladder are right upper quadrant and the appendix is right lower.

quiz.q: A chart entry reads LOC with no further detail. Why is this a documentation problem?
choices: It means loss of consciousness, which is never recorded with an abbreviation
It is on the Joint Commission do-not-use list
It can mean either loss of consciousness or level of consciousness, an event versus a measurement
It has no accepted meaning in emergency medicine
quiz.why: LOC is ambiguous between an event that happened and a measurement you took, which are entirely different claims about the patient. It is widely used and not on the official do-not-use list, which is exactly why the ambiguity persists.

quiz.q: A handoff states: 58F BIBA c/o CP x1h, hx MI, PMH CHF, NKDA, vitals WNL. Which statement is accurate?
choices: A 58-year-old female arrived by ambulance with one hour of chest pain, a history of heart attack and heart failure, no known drug allergies, and normal vital signs
A 58-year-old female arrived by private vehicle with one day of chest pain and known allergies
A 58-year-old male was brought in by ambulance after cardiac arrest with abnormal vitals
A 58-year-old female complains of chronic pain for one hour with an unknown medical history
quiz.why: BIBA is brought in by ambulance, c/o CP x1h is one hour of chest pain, hx MI and PMH CHF are prior heart attack and heart failure, NKDA is no known drug allergies, and WNL is within normal limits. The other options change the sex, the route of arrival, the duration, or the allergy status.

quiz.q: A patient with a suspected stroke was last seen normal at 21:00 and found with slurred speech at 05:30. Which time is documented as LKW and why?
choices: 05:30, because that is when symptoms were discovered
21:00, because last known well is the last moment the patient was verified normal
The midpoint, 01:15, because the exact onset is unknown
The time of the 911 call, because that starts the record
quiz.why: Last known well is the last verified normal moment, which is 21:00, and it is what determines treatment eligibility. Discovery time, a calculated midpoint, and the call time all overstate how recently the patient was well.

quiz.q: An order reads: ceftriaxone 1 g IV STAT. How quickly is it given, and by what route?
quiz.why: STAT is from statim, meaning immediately, and IV is intravenous. PRN is as needed, IM is intramuscular, and neither a frequency nor an oral route appears anywhere in the order.

quiz.q: An order is written as levothyroxine .05 mg PO daily. What is the risk and the correction?
choices: The dose is too small; increase it to 5 mg
A missing leading zero can be read as 5 mg, so write 0.05 mg
A trailing zero can be read as 500 mcg, so write .5 mg
The route is missing, so add PO
quiz.why: Without a leading zero the decimal point can be missed and .05 read as 5, a hundredfold error. The rule is always write a leading zero and never a trailing one. The route PO is already present, and no clinician changes a dose to fix a formatting problem.

quiz.q: A handwritten order reads MSO4 2 mg IV q2h PRN. What is the correct action?
choices: Give it as morphine, since MSO4 conventionally means morphine sulfate
Give it as magnesium, since the dose fits magnesium
Clarify with the prescriber, because MSO4 and MgSO4 are confused with each other and both are banned
Transcribe it into the record exactly as written and proceed
quiz.why: MSO4 and MgSO4 are on the do-not-use list precisely because they are mistaken for one another, and a banned abbreviation is clarified, never interpreted. Guessing from convention or from the dose is the failure mode the rule exists to prevent, and copying it forward propagates the hazard.

quiz.q: Why is mcg written out rather than the Greek mu symbol?
choices: The symbol is not recognized internationally
The symbol can be mistaken for mg, a thousandfold error
The symbol means milligram in some systems
The symbol is only valid for intravenous drugs
quiz.why: The handwritten mu symbol is read as an m, turning micrograms into milligrams, a thousandfold overdose. The symbol is internationally defined and route independent, so the problem is legibility rather than meaning.

quiz.q: Which order line contains no banned abbreviation?
choices: Acetaminophen 650 mg PO every 6 hours as needed for pain
Magnesium 2 g IV, written as MgSO4 2 g IV
quiz.why: The acetaminophen order spells the frequency out, has no trailing zero, and uses no banned symbol. U for unit, a trailing zero with QD for daily, and MgSO4 are each specifically listed as unsafe.

quiz.q: A patient's chart lists both cyanosis and a melanoma biopsy. Which color roots are at work?
quiz.why: Cyan/o is blue, so cyanosis is a blue condition of skin or mucous membranes, and melan/o is black, which names the dark pigmented tumor. Erythr/o is red and leuk/o is white, and neither appears in these two words.

quiz.q: A radiology report notes atelectasis at the left base. Using the suffix, what is being described?
choices: Incomplete expansion or collapse of lung
quiz.why: -ectasis refers to expansion, and atelectasis names lung that is not expanded, meaning collapsed or unexpanded. Narrowing is -stenosis, fluid in a space is an effusion, and hardening would be a -sclerosis ending.

quiz.q: A patient is described as having xerostomia and onychomycosis. What two problems is the chart naming?
choices: Dry mouth and a fungal nail infection
Painful mouth and a bruised nail
Mouth ulcers and a nail deformity from trauma
Excess saliva and a nail bed infection from bacteria
quiz.why: Xer/o is dry and stoma is mouth, giving dry mouth; onych/o is nail and myc/o is fungus, giving a fungal nail infection. Pain would be -algia, trauma is not a root here, and excess saliva is the opposite of xer/o.

quiz.q: A note describes hypertrophy of the left ventricle in one patient and atrophy of the thigh muscles in another. What does the shared suffix mean?
choices: Inflammation, in excess and in deficiency
Development or nourishment, excessive in one and absent in the other
quiz.why: -trophy is development or nourishment, so hyper- gives overgrowth and a- gives wasting. Inflammation is -itis, hardening is -sclerosis, and motion is not what this suffix carries.

quiz.q: A complete blood count shows a white cell count of 18,000 with increased bands. What is the term for the band increase and what does it suggest?
choices: Left shift, suggesting the marrow is releasing immature neutrophils early to fight infection
Right shift, suggesting a chronic viral illness
quiz.why: Bands are immature neutrophils, and their rise is called a left shift, which points to an active infection. Hemolysis is red cell breakage in the specimen, pancytopenia is a deficiency of all lines, and there is no standard right shift finding used this way.

quiz.q: Which single laboratory test most directly asks whether tissue is running without enough oxygen?
quiz.why: Lactate rises when tissue metabolizes without adequate oxygen, so it is the perfusion question. BNP asks whether the heart is stretched, D-dimer asks about clot breakdown, and INR measures clotting speed.

quiz.q: A CT report describes free air under the diaphragm. What does that finding suggest?
choices: Fluid filling alveoli, as in pneumonia
Air outside a hollow organ, suggesting perforation
quiz.why: Free air is air outside a hollow organ, which implies a perforation somewhere in the gastrointestinal tract. Alveolar filling is an infiltrate or consolidation, collapse is atelectasis, and an enlarged heart shadow is cardiomegaly.

quiz.q: An order reads: Amoxicillin 500 mg PO TID x 10 days. How many capsules are dispensed?
quiz.why: TID is three times daily, so three capsules for ten days is thirty. Ten would be once daily, twenty would be twice daily, and forty would be four times daily.

quiz.q: A hospitalized patient is ordered an antibiotic q8h rather than TID. What practical difference does the choice make?
choices: TID gives more total drug per day than q8h
q8h spaces doses evenly around the clock, including overnight, while TID clusters them in waking hours
q8h means only when the patient is awake
There is no difference; the two are interchangeable
quiz.why: q8h is every eight hours around the clock and will wake the patient, which keeps blood levels even; TID is three waking doses that may cluster. Both give three doses a day, so the totals match and the schedules do not.

quiz.q: A sig reads: prednisolone 15 mg PO ac. When is it taken?
quiz.why: ac is ante cibum, before meals. At bedtime is qhs, as the patient wishes is ad lib, and around the clock is ATC. After meals would be pc.

quiz.q: A fluid order reads: NS at 75 mL/hr, tubing drop factor 15 gtts/mL. Which two pieces of that order are shorthand you must decode before setting a rate?
choices: NS as normal saline and gtts as drops per minute for drip calculation
NS as nasogastric and gtts as grams
NS as no solution and gtts as gauge
NS as normal saline and gtts as gastric tube type
quiz.why: NS is normal saline and gtts are drops, with the drop factor printed on the tubing package converting an hourly volume into drops per minute. NG is nasogastric, grams are g, and gauge and tube type are not written as gtts.

quiz.q: A patient with a large pleural effusion has a needle placed to drain fluid, with no tube left behind. What is the procedure called?
quiz.why: -centesis is a puncture to withdraw fluid, so a needle drainage of the pleural space is thoracentesis. A thoracostomy leaves a chest tube, a thoracotomy opens the chest surgically, and a pleurodesis fuses the pleural surfaces together.

quiz.q: A patient with rising pressure in a swollen lower leg after a crush injury goes to surgery. Which procedure name fits what is done?
quiz.why: A fasciotomy cuts the fascia to relieve compartment pressure. Arthrodesis fuses a joint, lithotripsy crushes a stone, and herniorrhaphy sews a hernia closed; none of those relieves pressure in a compartment.

quiz.q: A consent form lists a percutaneous coronary intervention. What does the word percutaneous tell you about the approach?
choices: The chest will be opened with a full incision
The procedure passes through a natural body opening
Small ports and a camera will be used in the abdomen
The vessel is reached through the skin with a catheter, with no surgical incision
quiz.why: Per- is through and cutane/o is skin, so percutaneous means through the skin with a needle or catheter. A full incision is open, small abdominal ports are laparoscopic, and through a natural opening is endoscopic.

quiz.q: A patient with fever and neck stiffness flexes the hips and knees involuntarily when you flex the neck. What is this called?
quiz.why: Neck flexion producing hip and knee flexion is Brudzinski's sign, one of the two meningeal irritation signs. Kernig's is pain on straightening the knee with the hip flexed, Babinski is the upgoing toe, and Chvostek's is facial twitching from low calcium.

quiz.q: A patient found outside in the cold has a hump at the end of the QRS complex on the monitor. What is that wave called and what does it suggest?
choices: A delta wave, suggesting an accessory pathway
An Osborn or J wave, suggesting hypothermia
quiz.why: The Osborn or J wave is the hump at the QRS-ST junction seen in hypothermia, which fits the exposure history. Levine's sign is a clenched fist over the sternum, not an ECG wave, and there is no Kussmaul wave; Kussmaul names a breathing pattern and a neck vein sign.

quiz.q: A patient in diabetic ketoacidosis is breathing deeply and rapidly with a sighing quality. What is that pattern called?
quiz.why: Kussmaul respirations are the deep, fast, sighing breaths of metabolic acidosis, classically diabetic ketoacidosis, as the body blows off carbon dioxide. Cheyne-Stokes cycles between deep and shallow with pauses in severe brain injury or end-stage illness, and agonal breaths are the irregular gasps near death.

quiz.q: A run sheet reads: Pt found seated tripod, A&Ox4, accessory muscle use, unable to speak full sentences. What do those four fragments describe together?
choices: An alert patient with significant work of breathing
A confused patient with a normal respiratory effort
An alert patient with a purely cardiac complaint
quiz.why: A&Ox4 means alert and oriented to person, place, time and event, while tripod posture, accessory muscle use and broken sentences are all work-of-breathing findings. The patient is neither confused nor unresponsive, and nothing in the line points to a cardiac cause.

quiz.q: You give a handoff and the receiving nurse asks what you want. Which structure would have prevented that question?
quiz.why: SBAR ends with an explicit Recommendation, the specific ask, which is the part people most often leave unsaid. CHART and SOAP organize the narrative but do not force a request, and ROS is a review of symptoms, not a handoff format.

quiz.q: An ED note reads: MDM: COPD exacerbation vs acute CHF; BNP pending. What is this section telling you?
choices: The final diagnosis has been made and is COPD
The differential the physician is weighing and the test that will separate the two
The discharge instructions given to the patient
The review of systems collected on arrival
quiz.why: Medical decision making holds the reasoning and the differential, and vs marks two competing explanations with BNP ordered to separate them. Nothing is final, discharge belongs in disposition, and the review of systems is a separate earlier section.

quiz.q: A patient who left before an evaluation began is charted with which abbreviation?
quiz.why: LWBS is left without being seen, which is the patient who never had the evaluation. AMA is leaving against medical advice after being seen, MCI is a mass casualty incident, and POV means arrival by privately owned vehicle.

quiz.q: You are given a verbal order for 15 mg of a medication over a noisy radio. What is the safest way to confirm it?
choices: Repeat it as one-five milligrams and wait for confirmation
Write it down and give it, since the order was clear
Ask for the dose in grams instead
Confirm it with a partner rather than the prescriber
quiz.why: Fifteen and fifty are routinely confused over a radio, so saying one-five and getting a read-back confirmation closes the entire class of mishearing errors. Acting without confirmation, converting units, and asking a bystander all leave the original ambiguity in place.

quiz.q: An exam stem describes an infection of the membranes covering the brain and cord and asks for the term. Which neurologic root set gives it to you?
quiz.why: Mening/o names the membranes covering the brain and spinal cord, so with -itis it gives meningitis. Encephal/o is the brain itself, neur/o is a peripheral nerve, and myel/o is the cord or marrow rather than its coverings.

quiz.q: A gastrointestinal stem describes inflammation of the sac that stores bile. Which two roots do you retrieve and what word do they build?
quiz.why: Chol/e is bile and cyst/o is the sac, so with -itis they build cholecystitis, inflammation of the gallbladder. Cholelithiasis is gallstones rather than inflammation, hepatomegaly is an enlarged liver, and gastroenteritis involves stomach and small intestine.
